title: The glorious mysteries
hookLine: resurrection, ascension, Pentecost, assumption, Mary crowned (Wednesdays and Sundays)
last: WALK THE HARD ROAD WITH HIM.

lines: THE BEADS DON'T STOP AT THE TOMB.
cards: Some people read the last page of a novel first. They want to know it ends all right before they can bear the middle. The rosary, in a way, lets you do that.
Yesterday's beads left Jesus on the cross, then in the tomb. If they stopped there, it would be a prayer of grief. They don't.
On Wednesdays and Sundays, Catholics pick up the beads and pray the last page: five scenes of what happens after.

teach.h: HE IS NOT HERE, BUT IS RISEN.
teach.b: First, the resurrection. Women come to the tomb at dawn with spices, and it's empty. In the Douay-Rheims, the angels tell them, "He is not here, but is risen."

Second, the ascension: forty days later, Jesus is taken up out of the disciples' sight. Third, the descent of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost: wind, tongues like fire, and frightened people suddenly speaking in the street.
Those three are all in the Bible. The last two are about Mary, and here it's honest to say where they come from.
The fourth is the assumption: Catholics believe that at the end of her life Mary was taken up, body and soul, into heaven. The Bible doesn't describe this.
It's an old tradition, celebrated for centuries, and Pope Pius the Twelfth defined it as Catholic teaching in 1950.

The Orthodox keep a closely related feast called the Dormition, the falling asleep of Mary, and most Protestant churches don't hold the teaching. The fifth is the coronation: Mary crowned as queen of heaven.

Catholics often picture it through the book of Revelation, which the Douay-Rheims calls the Apocalypse: "a woman clothed with the sun, and the moon under her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars."
So what's the point of the five together?
The Greek word for glory is doxa, splendor, and behind it in the Bible stands the Hebrew kavod, which also means weight. Glory shines, and it's heavy.

teach.h: THE STORY ENDS HEAVY WITH LIGHT.
teach.b: The glorious mysteries say the story ends heavy with light. What happened to Jesus, Catholics say, is meant to happen to everyone: risen, taken home, crowned. Mary goes first, as the first disciple.
The end is glory, and the hard road leads there.

how: Catholics who pray the rosary usually meditate on the glorious mysteries on Wednesdays and Sundays, moving from the empty tomb to Mary crowned in heaven.

games.q: you're one of the women at the tomb at dawn, carrying spices. the stone is rolled back. what do you hear?
o: he has been taken away by the guards.
he is not here, but is risen.
games.why: "He is not here, but is risen." they came to anoint a body and ran back with news instead.

practice: Choose the first one, the empty tomb at dawn: picture the light coming up, and the women running back with the news.

Then think of one thing in your own life that felt finished and wasn't, a friendship that came back, a hope that returned. If you pray the rosary, pray the decade here; if you don't, just stay with the dawn.

wordCard.voice: Glorious mysteries. Resurrection, ascension, Pentecost, the assumption, Mary crowned. The last page, read on Wednesdays and Sundays. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: glory, splendor. In the Greek Bible it translates the Hebrew kavod, which also means weight, the heaviness of something real.
